title: Cache Eviction Policies
description: Explore LRU, LFU, FIFO, and ARC eviction policies with step-by-step animated examples showing how each one decides what to remove.

segments.text: Caches are finite. Eventually, they fill up and you have to decide what to throw away to make room for new data. That decision is your eviction policy, and choosing the right one is the difference between a fast system and a slow one.

FIFO — First In, First Out — is the simplest. Whatever entered the cache first gets evicted first, like a queue. Easy to implement, but it ignores how frequently or recently data was accessed. A hot item gets evicted just because it's old.

LRU — Least Recently Used — is the most popular policy. It evicts the item that hasn't been accessed for the longest time. The intuition is simple: if you haven't used it recently, you probably won't need it soon.

Let's walk through it. Cache has slots for three items. We access A, B, C — cache is full. Now we access A again — A moves to the front. We need to add D — C is least recently used, so C gets evicted. D takes its place.
LRU uses a hash map plus a doubly linked list under the hood. That gives you O of one for both lookups and evictions. Elegant engineering.
segments.thought_prompt: Can you think of a scenario where LRU would perform poorly? What access pattern would trick it?

segments.text: LRU fails with scan patterns. If you sequentially scan through a dataset larger than your cache, every item gets accessed once and then evicted. Your cache becomes useless — you're constantly evicting things you just added.

LFU — Least Frequently Used — tracks how many times each item is accessed. The item with the lowest count gets evicted. It handles scans better because frequently accessed items have high counts that protect them.

But LFU has its own weakness. An item that was popular an hour ago still has a high count even if nobody uses it anymore. It's stale but protected. LFU has a hard time adapting to changing access patterns.

ARC — Adaptive Replacement Cache — combines the best of both. It maintains two LRU lists: one for recency and one for frequency. It dynamically adjusts the balance between them based on observed workload patterns.

ARC also keeps ghost entries — metadata about recently evicted items. If an evicted item is requested again, ARC learns from that miss and shifts its balance. It's self-tuning. ZFS and IBM use it extensively.

So which policy should you use? For most web applications, LRU is the right default. It's simple, fast, and works well for temporal locality. Only reach for LFU or ARC when you have evidence that LRU isn't cutting it.
segments.thought_prompt: If you were building a CDN serving both popular and long-tail content, which eviction policy would you choose?

segments.text: Eviction policies are the brain of your cache. FIFO is naive, LRU is practical, LFU is frequency-aware, and ARC is adaptive. Understanding their tradeoffs lets you tune caching for your specific workload. Next, let's dive deep into Redis.
